*Abstract*: Learning continually while not forgetting is a long-standing pursuit of machine learning systems (Kumaran et al., 2016; McClelland et al., 1995; Arani et al., 2022). Incremental learning, or continual learning is such a fabulous way to train a model with continuously expanded datasets by adding novel classes or domains (Ring, 1997; Hadsell et al., 2020; De Lange et al., 2021). In general, continual learning includes two distinct settings, i.e., class- and task-incremental learning (Van de Ven & Tolias, 2019), abbreviated as CIL and TIL respectively. The main difference is whether the task identifier, i.e., the samples belong to which training tasks, is given for inference. 

Recently, the appearance of the prompt-tuning paradigm provides a new sight for class-incremental learning (Wang et al., 2022a; Li et al., 2023). In this framework, a tiny set of trainable tokens, i.e., prompts, are combined with image features, and forwarded into a fixed Transformer architecture. As the instance-wise query mechanism can select relevant prompts according to the input sample, only these relevant parts are updated during training (Wang et al., 2022c). Since the idea of prompt-tuning is borrowed from the area of natural language processing (NLP) (Lester et al., 2021; Li & Liang, 2021), its deep mechanism against forgetting has not been revealed yet (Zhou et al., 2023). 

Fortunately, it is observed that learning would not forget if the gradient is updated in the orthogonal direction to the subspace spanned by the old inputs, i.e., gradient projection approaches (GP) (Saha et al., 2021). However, one obvious limitation is that GP is only applicable for task incremental learning, because the gradient constraints would greatly restrict the learning of new tasks compared with normal training (Zhao et al., 2023). Thus, it needs task identifier to instruct updating. 

Based on this observation, we propose to combine prompt-tuning and gradient projection for further anti-forgetting. This combination enjoys: i) prompt-tuning with the instance-wise query mechanism releases the limitation of task identifier for gradient projection; ii) gradient projection provides the theoretical guarantees against forgetting for prompt-tuning. 

In this paper, we propose a novel prompt gradient projection (PGP) for continual learning. We recall the pipeline of prompt-based continual learning (prompt-tuning) and deduce the orthogonal condition of anti-forgetting for prompt gradient via the self-attention mechanism in vision-transformer. We solve the condition equations by conducting Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) on an element-wise sum space between input space and prompt space. That allows us to obtain the gradient projection matrix in an efficient way. 

We validate our approach in four benchmark datasets: CIFAR-100, ImageNet-R, TinyImageNet, and CUB200, with three baselines of L2P (Wang et al., 2022c), DualPrompt (Wang et al., 2022b), and CLIP (Radford et al., 2021), where an extraordinary anti-forgetting property is observed shown in Figure 1. We are the first to explicitly provide anti-forgetting mechanism for prompt-based continual learning, and hope our study will further inspire follow-up works. Our contributions are: 

(1) Prompt gradient projection is the first work to study the anti-forgetting mechanism of prompt-tuning. Our approach obtains the orthogonal condition of anti-forgetting for prompt gradient and hence the retention of old knowledge has a rigorous theoretical guarantee. 

(2) We provide a new viewpoint about stability and plasticity by investigating the selection of prompt gradient projection matrix. It appears that the essence of gradient projection is actually a trade-off, where the optimal solution is updating prompt in the orthogonal space of previous tasks. 

(3) We apply our approach in both prompt-tuning and prefix-tuning paradigms and show the effectiveness of our approach. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art results in terms of forgetting metric and average accuracy metric, under the settings of class incremental learning, online class incremental learning, and task incremental learning.

This paper proposes a hybrid distillation strategy to combine the strengths of contrastive learning and masked image modeling. The authors first examine previous feature distillation and mask feature reconstruction methods and identify their limitations. They find that their increasing diversity mainly derives from the asymmetric designs, but these designs may in turn compromise the discrimination ability. Furthermore, a progressive redundant token masking strategy is also utilized to reduce the distilling costs and avoid falling into local optima. ## Reviewer

### Summary

The authors propose a novel fine-tuning approach for LLMs that is specifically designed for the translation task, eliminating the need for the abundant parallel data that traditional translation models usually depend on. ### Summary

This paper proposes a novel link prediction model and further boost it by studying graph incompleteness. First, the paper introduces MPNN-then-SF, an innovative architecture leveraging structural feature (SF) to guide MPNN's representation pooling, with its implementation, namely Neural Common Neighbor (NCN). % This file provides the abstract, introduction, and conclusion for the paper "DiffMatch: Diffusion Models for Dense Correspondence" by Yoonjae Kim, Jaehyeong Choo, and Sungjin Kim.

\section{Abstract}

Establishing dense correspondence between paired images is a fundamental problem in computer vision, with applications in structure from motion, simultaneous localization and mapping, image editing, and video analysis. Traditional methods rely on hand-designed prior terms, which can be challenging to formulate and may vary depending on the specific task. Recent approaches focus on learning the data term with deep neural networks, but often struggle with inherent ambiguities in matching, such as textureless regions, repetitive patterns, large displacements, or noises. This paper introduces DiffMatch, a novel conditional diffusion-based framework that explicitly models both the data and prior terms for dense matching. The framework uses a conditional denoising diffusion model that takes matching cost and injects the prior within the generative process. To address the limited input resolution of the diffusion model, a cascaded pipeline is proposed, starting with a low-resolution model followed by a super-resolution model that upsamples and incorporates finer details to the matching field. Experimental results demonstrate significant performance improvements over existing approaches, and ablation studies validate the design choices and effectiveness of each component.

\section{Introduction}

Establishing pixel-wise correspondences between pairs of images is a crucial problem, supporting various applications, including structure from motion (SfM), simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), image editing, and video analysis. Unlike sparse correspondence, which detects and matches only a sparse set of key points, dense correspondence aims to match all the points between input images. The objective for dense correspondence can be defined with a data term, measuring matching evidence between source and target features, and a prior term, encoding prior knowledge of correspondence. Traditional methods explicitly incorporated hand-designed prior terms to achieve smoother correspondence, such as total variation (TV) or image discontinuity-aware smoothness. However, the formulation of the hand-crafted prior term is notoriously challenging and may vary depending on the specific dense correspondence tasks, such as geometric matching or optical flow.

Unlike them, recent approaches have focused on solely learning the data term with deep neural networks. However, despite demonstrating certain performance improvements, these methods still struggle with effectively addressing the inherent ambiguities encountered in dense correspondence, including challenges posed by textureless regions, repetitive patterns, large displacements, or noises. We argue that it is because they concentrate on maximizing the likelihood, which corresponds to learning the data term only, and do not explicitly consider the matching prior. This limits their ability to learn ideal matching field manifold, and leads to poor generalization.

On the other hand, diffusion models have recently demonstrated a powerful capability for learning posterior distribution and have achieved considerable success in the field of generative models. Inspired by the recent success of the diffusion model, we introduce DiffMatch, a conditional diffusion-based framework designed to explicitly model the matching field distribution within diffusion process. Unlike existing discriminative learning-based methods that focus solely on maximizing the likelihood, DiffMatch aims to learn the posterior distribution of dense correspondence. Specifically, this is achieved by a conditional denoising diffusion model designed to learn how to generate a correspondence field given feature descriptors as conditions. However, limited input resolution of the diffusion model is a significant hindrance. To address this, we adopt a cascaded diffusion pipeline, starting with a low-resolution diffusion model, and then transitioning to a super-resolution diffusion model that successively upsamples the matching field and incorporates higher-resolution details.

We evaluate the effectiveness of DiffMatch using several standard benchmarks, and show the robustness of our model with the corrupted datasets. We also conduct extensive ablation studies to validate our design choices and explore the effectiveness of each component.

\section{Related Work}

### Dense correspondence

Traditional methods for dense correspondence relied on hand-designed matching priors. Several techniques introduced optimization methods, such as SIFT Flow, which designed smoothness and small displacement priors, and DCTM, which introduced a discontinuity-aware prior term. However, manually designing the prior term is difficult. To address this, recent approaches have shifted to a learning paradigm, formulating an objective function to solely maximize likelihood. This assumes that an optimal matching prior can be learned from a large-scale dataset. DGC-Net and GLU-Net proposed a coarse-to-fine framework using a feature pyramid, while COTR employed a transformer-based network. GOCor developed a differentiable matching module to learn spatial priors, addressing matching ambiguities. PDC-Net+ presented dense matching using a probabilistic model, estimating a flow field paired with a confidence map. DKM introduced a kernel regression global matcher to find accurate global matches and their certainty.

### Diffusion models

Diffusion models have been extensively researched due to their powerful generation capability. The Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) proposed a diffusion model in which the forward and reverse processes exhibit the Markovian property. The Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM) accelerated DDPM by replacing the original diffusion process with non-Markovian chains to enhance the sampling speed. Building upon these advancements, conditional diffusion models that leverage auxiliary conditions for controlled image synthesis have emerged. Palette proposed a general framework for image-to-image translation by concatenating the source image as an additional condition. Similarly, InstructPix2Pix trains a conditional diffusion model using a paired image and text instruction, specifically tailored for instruction-based image editing. On the other hand, several studies have turned their attention to resolution enhancement, as the Cascaded Diffusion Model adopts a cascaded pipeline to progressively interpolate the resolution of synthesized images using the diffusion denoising process.

### Diffusion model for discriminative tasks

Recently, the remarkable performance of the diffusion model has been extended to solve discriminative tasks, including image segmentation, depth estimation, object detection, and pose estimation. These approaches have demonstrated noticeable performance improvement using diffusion models. Our method represents the first application of the diffusion model to the dense correspondence task.

\section{Preliminaries}

### Probabilistic interpretation of dense correspondence

Let us denote a pair of images, i.e., source and target, as $I_{\mathrm{src}}$ and $I_{\mathrm{tgt}}$ that represent visually or semantically similar images, and feature descriptors extracted from $I_{\mathrm{src}}$ and $I_{\mathrm{tgt}}$ as $D_{\mathrm{src}}$ and $D_{\mathrm{tgt}}$, respectively. The objective of dense correspondence is to find a correspondence field $F$ that is defined at each pixel ${i}$, which warps $I_{\mathrm{src}}$ towards $I_{\mathrm{tgt}}$ such that $I_{\mathrm{tgt}}({i}) \sim I_{\mathrm{src}}({i}+F({i}))$ or $D_{\mathrm{tgt}}({i}) \sim D_{\mathrm{src}}({i}+F({i}))$.

This objective can be formulated within probabilistic interpretation, where we seek to find $F^{*}$ that maximizes the posterior probability of the correspondence field given a pair of feature descriptors $D_{\mathrm{src}}$ and $D_{\mathrm{tgt}}$, i.e., $p(F|D_{\mathrm{src}},D_{\mathrm{tgt}})$. According to Bayes' theorem, the posterior can be decomposed such that $p(F|D_{\mathrm{src}},D_{\mathrm{tgt}}) \propto p(D_{\mathrm{src}},D_{\mathrm{tgt}}|F) \cdot p(F)$. To find the matching field $F^{*}$ that maximizes the posterior, we can use the maximum a posteriori (MAP) approach:
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
F^{*} &= \underset{F}{\mathrm{argmax}}\, p(F|D_{\mathrm{src}},D_{\mathrm{tgt}}) = \underset{F}{\mathrm{argmax}}\, p(D_{\mathrm{src}},D_{\mathrm{tgt}}|F) \cdot p(F) \\
&= \underset{F}{\mathrm{argmax}}\{
\underbrace{\log p(D_{\mathrm{src}},D_{\mathrm{tgt}}|F)}_{\textrm{data term}}
+\underbrace{\log p(F)}_{\textrm{prior term}}
\}.
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
In this probabilistic interpretation, the first term, referred to as data term, represents the matching evidence between feature descriptors $D_{\mathrm{src}}$ and $D_{\mathrm{tgt}}$, and the second term, referred to as prior term, encodes prior knowledge of the matching field $F$.

### Conditional diffusion models

The diffusion model is a type of generative model, and can be divided into two categories: unconditional models and conditional models. Specifically, unconditional diffusion models learn an explicit approximation of the data distribution, denoted as $p(X)$. On the other hand, conditional diffusion models estimate the data distribution given a certain condition $K$, e.g., text prompt, denoted as $p(X|K)$.

In the conditional diffusion model, the data distribution is approximated by recovering a data sample from the Gaussian noise through an iterative denoising process. Given a sample $X_0$, it is transformed to $X_t$ through the forward diffusion process at a time step $t\in \{T, T-1, \ldots, 1\}$, which consists of Gaussian transition at each time step $q(X_{t} | X_{t-1}) :=\mathcal{N}(\sqrt{1-\beta_t}X_{t-1}, \beta_t I)$. The forward diffusion process follows the pre-defined variance schedule $\beta_t$ such that
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:forward_ddpm}
X_t = \sqrt{{\alpha_t}}X_0  + \sqrt{1 - {\alpha_t}}{Z},\quad Z \sim \mathcal{N} (0,I),
\end{equation}
where $\alpha_t = \prod_{i=1}^{t}(1 - \beta_{i})$. After training, we can sample data from the learned distribution through iterative denoising with the pre-defined range of time steps, called the reverse diffusion process, following the non-Markovian process of DDIM, which is parametrized as another Gaussian transition $p_\theta(X_{t-1} \mid X_{t}):= \mathcal{N}(X_{t-1}; \mu_\theta(X_t, t), \sigma_{\theta}(X_t, t){I})$. To this end, the diffusion network $\mathcal{F}_{\theta}(X_t, t ;K)$ predicts the denoised sample $\hat{X}_{0,t}$ given $X_t$, $t$ and $K$. One step in the reverse diffusion process can be formulated such that

\label{eq:reverse_ddpm}

\end{equation}

The authors propose to learn a generative model to generate model parameters for the target city based on the source city's parameters and prompts. The proposed method is evaluated on two real-world datasets for crowd flow prediction and traffic speed prediction tasks. The results show that the proposed method outperforms the baseline methods.

### Soundness

2 fair

### Presentation

2 fair

### Contribution

2 fair

The idea of learning a generative model to generate model parameters for the target city is interesting and novel.

### Weaknesses

1. The motivation of the paper is not clear. Why do we need to learn a generative model to generate model parameters? What is the benefit of this approach? 

2. The experiments are not sufficient. The authors only evaluate the proposed method on two datasets. The results are not convincing.

3. The proposed method is not well-motivated. The authors claim that the proposed method is model-agnostic, but the experiments only show the results of one model. 

4. The paper is not well-written. The presentation is not clear. The figures are not clear. The authors should make sure that the paper is easy to follow.

See the weaknesses.

review.summary: This paper proposes a novel method for reconstructing a 3D object from a few unposed images with little visual overlap, while simultaneously estimating the relative camera poses. The proposed method uses a self-attention block to exchange information between 3D object tokens and 2D image tokens, predicts a coarse point cloud for each view, and then uses a differentiable Perspective-n-Point (PnP) solver to obtain camera poses. The method shows strong cross-dataset generalization ability and outperforms baseline methods in pose prediction accuracy and 3D reconstruction quality.

*Abstract*: In object detection, varying annotation protocols across datasets can result in annotation mismatches, leading to inconsistent class labels and bounding regions. Addressing these mismatches typically involves manually identifying common trends and fixing the corresponding bounding boxes and class labels. To alleviate this laborious process, we introduce the label transfer problem in object detection. Here, the goal is to transfer bounding boxes from one or more source datasets to match the annotation style of a target dataset. We propose a data-centric approach, Label-Guided Pseudo-Labeling (LGPL), that improves downstream detectors in a manner agnostic to the detector learning algorithms and model architectures. Validating across four object detection scenarios, defined over seven different datasets and three different architectures, we show that transferring labels for a target task via LGPL consistently improves the downstream detection in every setting, on average by $1.88$ mAP and $2.65$ AP$^{75}$. Most importantly, we find that when training with multiple labeled datasets, carefully addressing annotation mismatches with LGPL alone can improve downstream object detection better than off-the-shelf supervised domain adaptation techniques that align instance features.

*Abstract*
\vspace{-0.6em}
Typical deep visual recognition models are capable of performing the one task they were trained on.
In this paper, we tackle the extremely difficult problem of combining distinct models with different initializations, each solving a separate task, into one multi-task model \textbf{without any additional training}. Prior work in model merging permutes one model to the space of the other then averages them together. While this works for models trained on the same task, we find that this fails to account for the differences in models trained on disjoint tasks. Thus, we introduce ``ZipIt!'', a general method for merging two arbitrary models of the same architecture that incorporates two simple strategies. First, in order to account for features that aren't shared between models, we expand the model merging problem to allow for merging features \textit{within} each model by defining a general ``zip'' operation. Second, we add support for \textit{partially zipping} the models up until a specified layer, naturally creating a multi-head model. We find that these two changes combined account for 20-60\% improvement over prior work, 
making it more feasible to merge models trained on disjoint tasks \textit{without retraining}.

\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}


Ever since AlexNet \cite{krizhevsky2017imagenet} popularized deep learning in computer vision, the field has thrived under the reign of massive models with an ever increasing number of parameters. 
Many
vision problems once considered difficult or impossible are now benchmark tasks: classification with tens of thousands of classes \cite{deng2009imagenet,zhou2017scene,gemmeke2017audio}, 
fast instance segmentation \cite{he2017mask,bolya2019yolact}, realistic image generation \cite{karras2018style,ho2020denoising,rombach2022high}, and more.

There are an abundance of independent, carefully tuned models out there for many tasks.
However, if we want to expand an existing model's capabilities, we run into many potential issues. If we try training the model on an additional task, we face catastrophic forgetting \cite{kirkpatrick2017overcoming,li2017learning,de2021continual}. If we evaluate the same model on different data without adaptation, we often find it doesn't generalize to out of domain samples \cite{blanchard2011generalizing,muandet2013domain,wang2022generalizing}. We can try so called ``intervention'' strategies \cite{wang2022generalizing,de2021continual} to mitigate these effects, but these often require further training which can be expensive~\cite{dosovitskiy2020image,zhai2022scaling,dehghani2023scalingvit22b}. 
Instead, it would be nice if we could expand a model's capacity to solve new tasks by simply ``zipping'' it with other models trained on those tasks \textit{without additional training}.
\input{figures/0_concept_and_capabilities}

Combining multiple models into one has recently started to gain traction in the vision community.
Model Soups \cite{wortsman2022model} can add multiple models finetuned from the same pretrained initialization to improve accuracy and robustness. Git Re-Basin \cite{ainsworth2022git} generalizes further to models trained on the same data but with different initializations, though with a significant accuracy drop. REPAIR \cite{jordan2022repair} improves on Git Re-Basin by adding new parameters and adjusting model batch norms where applicable.
However, all of these methods only combine models trained on the same task.
In this paper, we take this line of work to a logical extreme: merging differently initialized models trained on \textit{completely separate} tasks (see Fig.~\ref{fig:concept_and_capabilities}\hyperref[fig:concept_and_capabilities]{ab}).
We show
that this is an incredibly difficult problem for prior work 
and
employ two simple strategies to make it feasible.

First, we note that prior work focuses on \textit{permuting} one model to the other when merging them. This creates a 1-1 mapping between the two models, inherently assuming that most features \textit{across} them are correlated. Since this isn't necessarily the case for models trained on different tasks, we cannot rely on permutation alone. 
Instead, we generalize model merging to support ``zipping'' any combination of correlated features \textit{within} and \textit{across} each model.
We find that on some tasks, this alone improves accuracy \textbf{by up to 20\%} vs. 
permutation-based approaches.
Moreover, we prove that merging within models can yield a better result in the theoretical setting of \citet{entezari2021role}.

Second, existing methods merge \textit{the entire network}. While this might work for extremely similar models trained in the same setting, the features of models trained on disjoint tasks become less correlated over the course of the network \cite{kornblith2019similarity}. To solve this, we introduce \textit{partial zipping}, where we only ``zip'' up to a specified layer. Afterward, we feed the merged model's outputs to the remaining unmerged layers of the original networks, creating a multi-head model. Depending on task difficulty, this can improve accuracy \textbf{by over 15\%} while still keeping most layers merged.
Incorporating both of these strategies, we introduce \name{}\ (Fig.~\ref{fig:concept_and_capabilities}\hyperref[fig:concept_and_capabilities]{c}), a general method for ``zipping'' any number of models trained on different tasks into a single multitask model \textit{without retraining}.
By deriving a general graph-based algorithm for merging and unmerging (Sec.~\ref{sec:approach}), we can zip models of the same architecture together, 
merge features \textit{within} each model,
and partially zip them to create a multi-task model.
We validate our approach by merging models trained on entirely disjoint sets of CIFAR \cite{krizhevsky2009cifar} and ImageNet \cite{deng2009imagenet} categories, as well as merging several models trained on completely independent datasets into one, significantly outperforming prior work (Sec.~\ref{sec:results}). 
Finally, we ablate and analyze our method's capabilities on these scenarios (Sec.~\ref{sec:ablations}).

%
% Model merging combines the weights of two or more models into a one. Our work differs from prior work in that we adapt mode connectivity techniques to target models trained on disjoint tasks. Merging Finetuned Models If two models are finetuned from the same pretrained checkpoint, they often lie in the same error basin. Several works have exploited this property to average together the weights of a model at different stages of training. Merging Differently Initialized Models Merging models with different initializations is a much more challenging problem. Works in this space often rely on mode connectivity, attempting to interpolate between models along a low loss path. Most recent work follow the intuition, later formalized by Entezari et al., that models permuted to the same loss basin can be merged by averaging their weights. % Model merging stems from mode connectivity, where it is conjectured that models trained with SGD on the same dataset lying in the same loss basin (i.e., region or mode of low loss) can be combined into a single model that's just as performant as the original models. First, in order to account for features that aren't shared between models, we expand the model merging problem to allow for merging features \textit{within} each model by defining a general ``zip'' operation. Second, we add support for \textit{partially zipping} the models up until a specified layer, naturally creating a multi-head model. REPAIR \cite{jordan2022repair} improves on Git Re-Basin by adding new parameters and adjusting model batch norms where applicable.
However, all of these methods only combine models trained on the same task.
In this paper, we take this line of work to a logical extreme: merging differently initialized models trained on \textit{completely separate} tasks (see Fig.~\ref{fig:concept_and_capabilities}\hyperref[fig:concept_and_capabilities]{ab}).

This creates a 1-1 mapping between the two models, inherently assuming that most features \textit{across} them are correlated. Since this isn't necessarily the case for models trained on different tasks, we cannot rely on permutation alone.

The paper studies the influence of scale on structure learning algorithms for DAGs. ## Reviewer
### Summary

The paper introduces a novel approach to variational inference called Variational Importance Sampling (VIS). The authors argue that variational inference (VI) can be improved by directly estimating and maximizing the log-likelihood, rather than relying on the evidence lower bound (ELBO) as in traditional VI. VIS uses the optimal proposal distribution, obtained by minimizing the forward $\chi^2$ divergence, to enhance log-likelihood estimation. The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of VIS on various latent variable models, including mixture models, variational autoencoders, and partially observable generalized linear models.

### Soundness

3 good

### Presentation

3 good

### Contribution

3 good

### Strengths

The paper introduces a novel approach to variational inference called Variational Importance Sampling (VIS). VIS directly estimates and maximizes the log-likelihood, rather than relying on the evidence lower bound (ELBO) as in traditional VI. This approach is motivated by the observation that the ELBO can be a poor approximation of the true log-likelihood when the posterior distribution is complex or multi-modal. By using the optimal proposal distribution, obtained by minimizing the forward $\chi^2$ divergence, VIS aims to improve the accuracy of log-likelihood estimation.

The authors demonstrate the effectiveness of VIS on various latent variable models, including mixture models, variational autoencoders, and partially observable generalized linear models. The experiments show that VIS consistently outperforms traditional VI and other state-of-the-art methods in terms of log-likelihood and model parameter estimation. The authors also provide a thorough analysis of the bias and variance of the VIS estimator, which provides insights into the trade-offs involved in using VIS.

The paper is well-written and easy to follow. The authors provide a clear explanation of the VIS algorithm and its connection to traditional VI. The experiments are well-designed and the results are presented in a clear and concise manner.

### Weaknesses

The paper could benefit from a more detailed discussion of the limitations of VIS. While the authors acknowledge that VIS may not be suitable for all types of models or datasets, they do not provide a more comprehensive analysis of the limitations of their approach. For example, it is not clear how VIS would perform on models with high-dimensional latent variables or on datasets with complex dependencies between variables.

The paper could also benefit from a more detailed comparison with other methods for improving VI. While the authors compare VIS with traditional VI and other state-of-the-art methods, they do not provide a more comprehensive comparison with other approaches for improving VI. For example, it would be interesting to see how VIS compares with other methods that use alternative divergence measures, such as the $\alpha$-divergence or the Wasserstein distance.

Finally, the paper could benefit from a more detailed discussion of the computational costs associated with VIS. While the authors acknowledge that VIS requires more computational resources than traditional VI, they do not provide a more detailed analysis of the computational costs involved. For example, it would be interesting to see how the computational costs of VIS compare with other methods for improving VI.

### Questions

1. How does VIS perform on models with high-dimensional latent variables?
2. How does VIS compare with other methods that use alternative divergence measures, such as the $\alpha$-divergence or the Wasserstein distance?
3. What are the computational costs associated with VIS?
4. How does VIS perform on datasets with complex dependencies between variables?

No ethics review needed.

### Summary

The authors propose a new approach to learning latent variable models, which they call variational importance sampling (VIS). The idea is to use importance sampling to estimate the marginal likelihood, and to learn the parameters by maximizing this estimate. The authors show that the optimal proposal distribution for importance sampling is the one that minimizes the forward $\chi^2$ divergence between the true posterior and the variational distribution. They also provide a gradient estimator for this objective. The authors evaluate their approach on three models: a mixture model, a VAE, and a partially observable generalized linear model. They compare their approach to several baselines, including variational inference (VI) and importance-weighted autoencoders (IWAE).

The authors also provide a gradient estimator for the objective of minimizing the forward $\chi^2$ divergence. The experiments demonstrate that VIS outperforms VI and IWAE on the three models considered.

### Weaknesses

The paper could benefit from a more thorough discussion of the limitations of the proposed approach. For example, the authors note that VIS requires a large number of samples to achieve good performance, which can be computationally expensive. It would be helpful to have a more detailed discussion of the computational costs associated with VIS, and to compare them to the costs of VI and IWAE. review.summary:
The authors study the problem of solving finite-sum monotone inclusions, where the goal is to find $x_* \in \mathbb{R}^d$ such that
$$
0 \in F(x_*) + G(x_*).
$$
Here, $F:\mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}^d$ is a single-valued, monotone, and Lipschitz map, and $G:\mathbb{R}^d \rightrightarrows \mathbb{R}^d$ is a maximally monotone and possibly multi-valued map. The authors consider the setting where $F$ has a finite-sum structure, meaning that it can be expressed as
$$
F(x) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n F_i(x).
$$
The authors assume access to the resolvent of $\eta G$ for $\eta > 0$, meaning that for any $x$ we can find $\bar{x}$ such that
$$
x - \bar{x} \in \eta G(\bar{x}).
$$
The authors measure oracle complexity of an algorithm in terms of oracle evaluations of component operators $F_i$ and the resolvent operator of $\eta G$.

The authors propose variants of the classical Halpern iteration that employ variance reduction to obtain improved complexity guarantees in which $n$ component operators in the finite sum are either cocoercive or Lipschitz continuous and monotone, with parameter $L$. The resulting oracle complexity of their methods, which provide guarantees for the last iterate and for a (computable) operator norm residual, is $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(n + \sqrt{n}L\varepsilon^{-1})$, which improves upon existing methods by a factor up to $\sqrt{n}$. This constitutes the first variance reduction-type result for general finite-sum monotone inclusions and for more specific problems such as convex-concave optimization when operator norm residual is the optimality measure. The authors further argue that, up to poly-logarithmic factors, this complexity is unimprovable in the monotone Lipschitz setting; i.e., the provided result is near-optimal.

### Summary

The paper proposes a method for fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) by adaptively selecting the most important tensors for training. The method is based on a dynamic programming algorithm that maximizes the training loss reduction while keeping the FLOPs within a user-specified ratio of the full fine-tuning FLOPs. The method is evaluated on several LLMs and datasets, and shows that it can achieve better accuracy and FLOPs reduction compared to existing methods.

3 good

2 fair

2 fair

- The paper addresses an important problem of fine-tuning LLMs in an energy-efficient way.
- The proposed method is based on a solid formulation of the problem and a dynamic programming algorithm.
- The method is evaluated on several LLMs and datasets, and shows promising results.

### Weaknesses

- The paper is not easy to follow. The method is not clearly explained, and the formulation is not well-defined. 
- The evaluation is limited to a few LLMs and datasets, and the results are not convincing.
- The paper does not discuss the limitations of the method and the potential drawbacks of using it.

### Summary

This paper proposes a new method called GreenTrainer for efficient fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) while reducing the computational cost. The main idea is to adaptively select the most appropriate set of LLM tensors for fine-tuning based on their importance and backpropagation cost in training. The authors propose a novel approach to quantify the contribution of each tensor update to the training loss using first-order Taylor expansion over the training loss. They also develop a dynamic programming (DP) algorithm to find the nearly optimal tensor selection from an exponential number of possibilities. The proposed method is evaluated on three open-sourced LLMs, OPT, BLOOMZ, and FLAN-T5, on text generation datasets, including SciTLDR and DialogSum. The results show that GreenTrainer can save up to 64% training FLOPs compared to full LLM fine-tuning without any noticeable accuracy loss. Compared to existing techniques such as Prefix Tuning and LoRA, GreenTrainer can achieve up to 4% improvement of model accuracy with the same amount of FLOPs reduction.

### Contribution

3. The proposed method can achieve up to 4% improvement of model accuracy with the same amount of FLOPs reduction compared to existing techniques such as Prefix Tuning and LoRA.

### Weaknesses

1. The proposed method is complex and requires a lot of computational resources to calculate the tensor importance and select the appropriate tensors for fine-tuning.
2. The proposed method may not be applicable to all types of LLMs and datasets, and may require additional tuning and hyperparameter optimization for different applications.
3. The evaluation of the proposed method is limited to three open-sourced LLMs, OPT, BLOOMZ, and FLAN-T5, on text generation datasets, including SciTLDR and DialogSum. It would be interesting to see how the proposed method performs on other types of LLMs and datasets.

### Questions

1. How does the proposed method compare to other methods for efficient fine-tuning of LLMs, such as LoRA and Prefix Tuning?

### Summary

This paper presents a new approach to label DP, which is a variant of DP that only considers the privacy of the labels. The main idea is to use DP-SGD and then use a projection step to remove the noise added by DP-SGD, which is possible because DP-SGD adds noise to both the features and the labels. The projection step is done by projecting the gradient onto the span of the per-example per-class gradients, which can be computed using advanced auto-diff. The authors provide empirical results on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and Criteo, showing that the proposed method outperforms the previous baselines in the high-privacy regime.

### Soundness

3 good

- The empirical results show that the proposed method outperforms the previous baselines in the high-privacy regime.

### Weaknesses

- The privacy analysis is not clear. The authors claim that the projection step does not break the privacy amplification by subsampling, but it is not clear why. In fact, the projection step is done using the examples in the alternative batch $I_t^P$, which may contain the same examples as the batch $I_t^G$. Therefore, the final projected gradient may reveal information about $I_t^G$ and break the privacy amplification by subsampling.
- The authors do not compare the proposed method with the state-of-the-art label DP algorithms, such as [1,2]. It is not clear how the proposed method compares with these algorithms in terms of utility and privacy.

## Reviewer
### Summary

This paper proposes AutoVP, a framework for automating the design choices of visual prompting for image classification tasks. The proposed framework considers four design choices: input scaling, visual prompts, pre-trained models, and output label mapping strategies. The proposed framework is evaluated on 12 image classification datasets and compared to several baselines. The results show that the proposed framework outperforms the baselines in most cases.

### Soundness

2 fair

### Presentation

2 fair

### Contribution

2 fair

### Strengths

The paper proposes a framework that considers four design choices for visual prompting, which is a good step towards automating the design of visual prompting for image classification tasks.

### Weaknesses

1. The paper lacks a detailed analysis of the design choices made by the proposed framework. It would be helpful to understand which design choices are most important for each dataset and why.

2. The paper does not compare the proposed framework with other recent visual prompting methods, such as Convolutional Visual Prompting (CVPT) [1] and Visual Prompt Tuning (VPT) [2]. It would be helpful to compare the proposed framework with these methods to understand its advantages and disadvantages.

3. The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the computational cost of the proposed framework. It would be helpful to understand the computational cost of the framework and how it compares to other visual prompting methods.

[1] Convolutional Visual Prompting, CVPR 2023.

[2] Visual Prompt Tuning, CVPR 2023.

### Questions

1. How does the proposed framework compare to other visual prompting methods in terms of accuracy and computational cost?

2. Can the proposed framework be used for other types of visual tasks, such as object detection and segmentation?

3. How does the proposed framework handle cases where the source and target domains have different label spaces?

No ethics review needed.

5: marginally below the acceptance threshold

## Paper Decision Policy

1. If at least 5 papers are submitted to a track, the bar is set at 5: the 5 papers above the bar are accepted, other papers are rejected.
2. If there are 3-4 papers, the bar is set at 6: the 2 papers above the bar are accepted, one is accepted as a spotlight, other papers are rejected.
3. If there are less than 3 papers, the bar is set at 8: the papers above the bar are accepted, other papers are rejected.

### Policy (to be checked by PC chairs before final decision)

1. If a paper receives a paper decision (accept/accept (spotlight)/accept (oral))/reject, the authors can appeal the decision. The authors need to provide a clear and concise description of the reasons for their appeal, along with any supporting materials. The AC in charge of the paper will review the appeal and the original review comments, and make a decision on whether to accept or reject the appeal. 2. If a paper receives a poster/accept (spotlight) decision, the authors can ask for an oral decision. *Abstract*
In our era of enormous neural networks, empirical progress has been driven by the philosophy that *more is better.*
Recent deep learning practice has found repeatedly that larger model size, more data, and more computation (resulting in lower training loss) optimizing to near-interpolation improves performance. In this paper we give theoretical backing to these empirical observations by showing that these three properties hold in random feature (RF) regression, a class of models equivalent to shallow networks with only the last layer trained.

Concretely, we first show that the test risk of RF regression decreases monotonically with both the number of features and samples, provided the ridge penalty is tuned optimally. In particular, this implies that infinite width RF architectures are preferable to those of any finite width. We then proceed to demonstrate that, for a large class of tasks characterized by powerlaw eigenstructure, training to near-zero training loss is *obligatory:* near-optimal performance can *only* be achieved when the training error is much smaller than the test error. Grounding our theory in real-world data, we find empirically that standard computer vision tasks with convolutional neural kernels clearly fall into this class. Taken together, our results tell a simple, testable story of the benefits of overparameterization and overfitting in random feature models.

review.summary: The paper introduces Instruction-oriented Object Detection (IOD), a new task that enhances human-computer interaction by enabling object detectors to understand user instructions and locate relevant objects. The authors create a dataset called IOD-Bench, which consists of instruction-guided detections, along with specialized evaluation metrics. The authors leverage large-scale language models (LLMs) to generate a diverse set of instructions based on existing public object detection datasets, covering a wide range of real-world scenarios. The authors propose a model called Ins-DetCLIP, which harnesses the extensive knowledge within LLMs to empower the detector with instruction-following capabilities. Experimental results conducted on IOD-Bench demonstrate that their model consistently outperforms baseline methods that directly combine LLMs with detection models.

review.summary: This paper proposes a new spiking neuron model called Learnable Multi-hierarchical (LM-H) model to address the limitations of the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) model in deep-layer gradient calculation and capturing global information on the time dimension. The LM-H model dynamically regulates its membrane-related factors and offers the flexibility to adjust the extraction ratio between historical and current information. The authors theoretically demonstrate the effectiveness of the LM-H model and propose a progressive training algorithm tailored specifically for the LM-H model. The authors also devise an efficient training framework for the LM-H model, encompassing hybrid training and time-slicing online training. The authors validate the remarkable superiority of the LM-H model and training algorithm compared to previous state-of-the-art approaches through extensive experiments on various datasets.

The authors propose an auto-documentation procedure to make these abstractions interpretable and improve human readability. The paper evaluates Lilo on three inductive program synthesis benchmarks and shows that it solves more complex tasks and learns richer libraries than existing methods.

### Questions

- In section 2.1, the authors state that the LLM-based search procedure introduced in section 2.1 can match the accuracy of enumerative search. However, the results in Table 1 suggest that the LLM-based search procedure does not perform as well as the enumerative search procedure. Can the authors explain this discrepancy?
- In section 2.1, the authors state that the LLM-based search procedure is more computationally efficient than the enumerative search procedure. However, the results in Table 1 suggest that the enumerative search procedure is more computationally efficient than the LLM-based search procedure. Can the authors explain this discrepancy?

LILO: Library Induction with Language Observations
=====================================================

### Overview

While large language models (LLMs) now excel at code generation, a key aspect of software development is the art of refactoring: consolidating code into libraries of reusable and readable programs. In this paper, we introduce LILO, a neurosymbolic framework that iteratively synthesizes, compresses, and documents code to build libraries tailored to particular problem domains.

LILO combines LLM-guided program synthesis with recent algorithmic advances in automated refactoring from Stitch: a symbolic compression system that efficiently identifies optimal λ-abstractions across large code corpora. To make these abstractions interpretable, we introduce an auto-documentation (AutoDoc) procedure that infers natural language names and docstrings based on contextual examples of usage. In addition to improving human readability, we find that AutoDoc boosts performance by helping LILO's synthesizer to interpret and deploy learned abstractions. We evaluate LILO on three inductive program synthesis benchmarks for string editing, scene reasoning, and graphics composition. Compared to existing methods---including the state-of-the-art library learning algorithm DreamCoder---LILO solves more complex tasks and learns richer libraries that are grounded in linguistic knowledge.

### Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are growing highly adept at programming in many settings: completing partially-written code [1, 2, 3], conversing with human programmers [4, 5], and even solving competition-level programming puzzles [6, 7, 8, 9]. However, beyond solving the immediate task at hand, software engineers are concerned with building libraries that can be applied to entire problem domains.

To this end, a key aspect of software development is the art of refactoring [10, 11]: identifying abstractions that make the codebase more concise (consolidating shared structure), reusable (generalizing to new tasks), and readable (intuitive to other programmers). Solving this multi-objective optimization will require broadening the scope of existing code completion tools---which are already used by millions of programmers---to approach the problem of library learning.

In this paper, we combine language models with recent algorithmic advances in automated refactoring from the programming languages (PL) literature to learn libraries of reusable function abstractions. We introduce LILO, a neurosymbolic framework for Library Induction from Language Observations, which consists of three interconnected modules (Figure 1):

*   A dual-system synthesis module, which searches for solutions to programming tasks using two distinct methods: LLM-guided search imbues the system with strong domain-general priors, and enumerative search enables the discovery of domain-specific expressions;
*   A compression module, which identifies useful abstractions from the existing solution set via Stitch [12], a high-performance symbolic compression system;
*   An auto-documentation (AutoDoc) module, which generates human-readable function names and docstrings, yielding better interpretability and improving downstream LLM-guided search.

Our architecture draws inspiration from DreamCoder [13], an iterative Wake-Sleep algorithm that alternates between searching for solutions to programming tasks (Wake phase) and refactoring shared abstractions into a library (Sleep phase) that in turn helps to guide search. Unlike standard deep learning approaches, DreamCoder can make strong generalizations from just a handful of examples, and the model's conceptual knowledge is represented symbolically in the learned library. However, DreamCoder's search procedure is extremely computationally intensive, requiring more than two CPU-months just to learn a single domain (see [13], Appendix J). Much of this search time is spent "getting off the ground": discovering a basic set of abstractions that human programmers typically already know, or might be able to grok quickly based on having solved problems in other domains. Moreover, DreamCoder libraries are not necessarily interpretable, requiring both domain expertise and knowledge of lambda calculus to decipher.

To address these issues, LILO leverages LLMs in two novel ways: (1) to expedite the discovery of program solutions during search, and (2) to improve the interpretability of learned libraries through documentation. We evaluate LILO against a language-guided DreamCoder variant on three challenging program synthesis domains: string editing with regular expressions [14], scene reasoning on the CLEVR dataset [15], and graphics composition in the 2D Logo turtle graphics language [16]. On all three domains, LILO solves more tasks than DreamCoder and learns empirically richer libraries containing abstractions that are intractable to discover with existing methods. For instance, LILO learns the concept of a vowel (Figure 2), which is a key stepping-stone in the string editing domain that would otherwise require searching over $26^5$ possible disjunctions of character primitives. Unlike LLM-only baselines---which can solve similar tasks---LILO compresses this knowledge into symbolic abstractions that are useful for both traditional search methods and LLM-guided synthesis. Key to this neurosymbolic integration is our AutoDoc module, which not only improves interpretability, but also helps the LLM synthesizer use the library more effectively.

LILO illustrates how ideas and tools from the PL community can be integrated with recent breakthroughs in language models, representing a new evolution in a long line of work in inductive program synthesis, which we review below.

### Preliminaries: Program Search and Library Learning

#### Program Synthesis

In inductive program synthesis [17], we are given a library of primitives $\mathcal{L} = \{ \mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2, \ldots \}$ that forms a domain-specific language (DSL). For a given programming task $\mathcal{T} = \{ (x_i, y_i) \}$ specified as a set of input-output pairs, the goal is to find a program $\mathbf{p} : \forall_i \mathbf{p}(x_i) = y_i$ that correctly maps all inputs to outputs, denoted $\mathbf{p} \vdash \mathcal{T}$. However, a typical task admits many such solutions that will not necessarily generalize (for instance, a simple lookup table). To address this inherent under-specification, concern is given to finding an optimal program $\hat{\mathbf{p}} \vdash \mathcal{T}$ with respect to descriptive complexity [18, 19, 20]. This optimization is naturally framed in terms of probabilistic inference:

$$\argmax_{\mathbf{p}} \log \mathbb{P}(\mathbf{p} \mid \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{L}) = \argmax_{\mathbf{p}} \left[ \log \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T} \mid \mathbf{p}) + \log \mathbb{P}(\mathbf{p} \mid \mathcal{L}) \right]$$

In a typical setting, the likelihood $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T} \mid \mathbf{p}) \triangleq \mathbbm{1}_{\mathbf{p} \vdash \mathcal{T}}$ is computed via program execution, while the prior $\mathbb{P}(\mathbf{p} \mid \mathcal{L}) \triangleq \prod_{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{P}} \mathbb{P}(\mathbf{p} \mid \mathcal{L})$ is defined under a probabilistic context free grammar (PCFG; [21]) that assigns a weight $0 \leq \theta \leq 1$ to each production rule. This is equivalent to a weighted description length prior, where longer programs have lower probability.

This formulation highlights the central challenge of program synthesis: historically, approaches to (1) have inevitably involved enumerative search through a combinatorial space of programs. A range of techniques have been proposed to improve search tractability, including type-directed synthesis [22], Monte Carlo approximation [23, 24, 25], and neural network guidance [26, 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32, 33, 34]. However, even with these methods, traditional program synthesis hinges critically on DSL design. Omission of key primitives can make complex tasks unsolvable, while inclusion of extraneous primitives can make search intractable. Consequently, DSL engineering is a painstaking process that requires significant expertise to anticipate common patterns across tasks in a domain.

#### Library Learning

While classical approaches focus on synthesizing the best program for a task specification given a fixed DSL (as in (1)), programmers in the wild are typically concerned with solving entire problem domains. Given the difficulty of manual DSL engineering, a natural evolution is to include $\mathcal{L}$ itself as part of the optimization problem. This is the main intuition behind library learning methods [35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40], which start with a collection of tasks $\mathcal{T} = \{ \mathcal{T}_1, \mathcal{T}_2, \ldots \}$ and a base library $\mathcal{L}_0$, and jointly infer an expanded library $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_0 \cup \mathcal{A}$ that includes additional abstractions $\mathcal{A}$ built from $\mathcal{L}_0$ (Figure 1B) and programs $\mathcal{P} = \{ \mathbf{p}_1, \mathbf{p}_2, \ldots \}$ written in terms of $\mathcal{L}$:

$$\argmax_{\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L}} \log \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L} \mid \mathcal{T}, \mathcal{L}_0) = \argmax_{\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{L}} \left[\sum_{\mathcal{T} \in \mathcal{T}} \log \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{T} \mid \mathbf{p}_\mathcal{T}) + \log \mathbb{P}(\mathbf{p}_\mathcal{T} \mid \mathcal{L}) \right] + \log \mathbb{P}(\mathcal{L} \mid \mathcal{L}_0)$$

This objective carries over the program prior and likelihood from (1), but introduces a distribution over libraries $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{L} \mid \mathcal{L}_0)$, typically also defined in terms of description length. Intuitively, (2) is optimized by inventing abstractions that are both reusable, simplifying the solutions to multiple tasks in $\mathcal{T}$; and concise, ideally building on one another hierarchically so as to share logic.

[35] approximate (2) via coordinate ascent, alternating between a search step, which holds the library fixed and searches for task solutions $\mathcal{P}$, and a refactoring step, which extracts common structure from the solution set to update $\mathcal{L}$. The tractability of this approach hinges critically on the ability to do efficient refactoring, which we discuss further in Section 3.2.

#### Leveraging Language Guidance

Given the size of the search space, generic priors such as description length are not always sufficient to solve (1); for this reason, a line of work considers natural language task descriptions $\mathcal{D}$ as an additional source of learning signal [36, 37, 38]. Traditionally, making use of such descriptions has required learning a domain-specific semantic parsing model [39, 40]. More recent work [41, 42, 43] uses LLMs, which excel when $\mathcal{L}$ resembles a common programming language that is well-represented in pretraining.

In library learning settings---where $\mathcal{L}$ is novel by construction---it is currently less clear how to leverage language. *Abstract*: 

Byzantine-robust distributed learning (BRDL), in which computing devices are likely to behave abnormally due to accidental failures or malicious attacks, has recently become a hot research topic. However, even in the independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) case, existing BRDL methods will suffer a significant drop on model accuracy due to the large variance of stochastic gradients. Increasing batch sizes is a simple yet effective way to reduce the variance. However, when the total number of gradient computation is fixed, a too-large batch size will lead to a too-small iteration number (update number), which may also degrade the model accuracy. In view of this challenge, we mainly study the effect of batch size when the total number of gradient computation is fixed in this work

review.summary: The paper proposes a method for text-to-speech generation conditioned on text prompts. The method is based on a combination of a diffusion model and a large language model. The diffusion model is used to generate a latent representation of the text prompt, which is then used to generate speech. The large language model is used to generate text prompts from speech attributes. The authors evaluate their method on a dataset of 44K hours of speech and demonstrate that it outperforms previous methods in terms of speech quality and attribute control.

The novelty of the paper lies in the combination of these two ideas and the specific implementation details, but these details are not sufficiently novel to warrant publication at ICLR.

## Reviewer
### Summary

This paper proposes a unified framework for human-scene interaction (HSI) that supports versatile interaction control through language commands. The framework defines interaction as a "Chain of Contacts (CoC)", representing steps involving human joint-object part pairs. The framework consists of a Large Language Model (LLM) Planner and a Unified Controller. The LLM Planner translates language prompts into task plans in the form of CoC, while the Unified Controller executes these plans. The authors also introduce a new dataset named ScenePlan that encompasses thousands of task plans generated by LLMs based on diverse scenarios. The experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework in versatile task execution and generalizability to real scanned scenes.

### Soundness

3 good

### Presentation

3 good

### Contribution

2 fair

### Strengths

1. The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
2. The idea of using a chain of contacts to represent human-scene interaction is interesting and novel.
3. The proposed framework is generalizable to various interaction tasks and can be trained without interaction annotations.
4. The experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the framework in versatile task execution and generalizability to real scanned scenes.

### Weaknesses

1. The paper lacks a detailed discussion of the limitations of the proposed method. For example, the method only supports fixed objects and does not consider moving or carrying objects. It also does not integrate LLM seamlessly into the training process.
2. The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the performance of the LLM Planner in generating accurate plans. The paper mentions that the LLM Planner may occasionally falter in spatial relations and devise plans involving object manipulation, but it does not provide a detailed analysis of the performance of the LLM Planner in generating accurate plans.
3. The paper does not provide a detailed discussion of the potential applications of the proposed framework. For example, how can the framework be used in real-world scenarios? What are the potential applications of the framework in fields such as virtual reality and robotics?
4. The paper does not provide a detailed analysis of the computational complexity of the proposed framework. For example, how long does it take to train the LLM Planner and the Unified Controller? How much computational resources are required to execute the framework in real-time?

### Questions

1. Can you provide more details on the limitations of the proposed method? For example, how does the method handle moving or carrying objects? How does the method integrate LLM seamlessly into the training process?
2. Can you provide more details on the performance of the LLM Planner in generating accurate plans? For example, what are the common mistakes made by the LLM Planner? How can these mistakes be addressed?
3. Can you provide more details on the potential applications of the proposed framework? For example, how can the framework be used in real-world scenarios? What are the potential applications of the framework in fields such as virtual reality and robotics?
4. Can you provide more details on the computational complexity of the proposed framework? For example, how long does it take to train the LLM Planner and the Unified Controller? How much computational resources are required to execute the framework in real-time?

No ethics review needed.

5: marginally below the acceptance threshold

The authors demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of their universal backdoor attacks by controlling models with up to 6,000 classes while poisoning only 0.15% of the training dataset.

## Reviewer

### Summary

This paper proposes a novel prototype-based tabular representation learning framework, PTaRL, for tabular prediction tasks. The framework involves two stages: Prototype Generation and Prototype Projection. The former constructs global prototypes as the basis vectors of P-Space for representation, while the latter projects data samples into P-Space and keeps the core global data information via Optimal Transport. To further acquire the disentangled representations, two strategies are proposed: diversification constraint for representation calibration and matrix orthogonalization constraint to avoid prototype entanglement. Experiments on various tabular benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of PTaRL.

### Soundness

2 fair

### Presentation

3 good

### Contribution

2 fair

### Strengths

1. The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
2. The proposed PTaRL framework is novel and interesting.
3. The experiments are extensive and convincing.

### Weaknesses

1. The motivation of this paper is not clear. The authors claim that the learned representations of existing deep tabular methods are usually entangled and cannot support clear and accurate decision-making, and each data sample are represented distinctively, making the global data structures over data samples are overlooked. However, the authors do not provide any evidence to support this claim. Besides, the authors do not explain why prototype learning can solve the entanglement and localization problems.
2. The experiments are not sufficient. The authors only conduct experiments on 6 datasets, which are small datasets. The authors should conduct experiments on more datasets, such as the datasets in OpenML, to verify the effectiveness of PTaRL. Besides, the authors should compare PTaRL with more baselines, such as DeepFM, xDeepFM, AutoInt, and so on.
3. The authors do not provide the implementation details of PTaRL, such as the hyperparameters of the framework, the hyperparameters of the backbone, and the training details.

### Questions

See the Weaknesses.

## Reviewer
### Summary

The authors present NLPBench, a benchmark for assessing the NLP-related problem-solving abilities of large language models (LLMs). NLPBench comprises 378 questions from Yale University's NLP course final exams, categorized into two types: with and without context, and three formats: multiple choice, short answer, and math. The authors evaluate five LLMs (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, PaLM-2, LLAMA-2 13b, and LLAMA-2 70b) using various prompting strategies, including zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought, and tree-of-thought. They find that GPT-4 outperforms other models, few-shot prompting is not always beneficial, and advanced prompting strategies are not consistently effective. The authors also conduct a manual analysis of errors, identifying weaknesses in logical decomposition, problem deduction, and logical reasoning. They conclude by recommending simple prompting methods, questioning the necessity of advanced strategies, and emphasizing the importance of training LLMs to enhance logical thinking skills.

### Soundness

2 fair

### Presentation

3 good

### Contribution

2 fair

### Strengths

1. The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
2. The authors present a comprehensive evaluation of LLMs on NLP-related problem-solving tasks, including multiple-choice, short-answer, and math questions.
3. The authors evaluate a variety of LLMs, including online and open-source models, and compare their performance under different prompting strategies.
4. The authors provide a detailed analysis of the errors made by LLMs, highlighting weaknesses in logical decomposition, problem deduction, and logical reasoning.

### Weaknesses

1. The paper lacks novelty in terms of the dataset and evaluation methodology. The authors use a standard approach to evaluate LLMs on NLP-related tasks, without introducing any new or innovative methods.
2. The dataset is relatively small, with only 378 questions from a single source (Yale University's NLP course final exams). This may limit the generalizability of the results.
3. The evaluation is limited to a single type of NLP task (NLP-related problem-solving). The authors do not evaluate LLMs on other types of NLP tasks, such as language understanding, generation, or translation.
4. The paper does not provide any insights into why the LLMs perform differently on different tasks or how the results can be used to improve LLMs.

## Reviewer

### Summary

This paper proposes a novel method to encode the subgraphs into the proposed GNN model. The proposed method stems from graph signal processing and spectral graph theory. The authors introduce a new eigenbasis, Learnable Lanczos Layer with Linear Constraints (LLwLC), that encodes the linear constraints, mainly the extracted subgraphs, into the basis. The authors devise their proposed low-rank approximation of the Laplacian matrix based on the Lanczos algorithm with linear constraints. The new basis makes the features more expressive by explicitly encoding the linear constraints over the graph. The authors investigate linear constraints with different subgraph extraction policies. The authors mainly conduct their experiments with the vertex-deleted subgraphs and Neumann eigenvalue constraints. The former is beneficial to show that LLwLC is a universal approximator (specifically with a few linear constraints). The latter is beneficial by encoding the boundary conditions of the input graph as new linear constraints into the eigenbasis (link representation between one hop and two hop away nodes leads to counting the triangle and substructures). The Neumann constraints let GNNs distinguish between the k-regular graphs from each other, as shown in Figure 1. Theoretically, LLwLC can be conducted in many problem settings. The authors analyze its effectiveness on challenging LP tasks where addressing k-regular graphs and counting the substructures are crucial for their success.

The results show that the proposed method can improve the accuracy of the global model while maintaining a low attack success rate.

In DP-FL, each party protects its local data by only submitting local model updates protected via strong DP guarantees. A central server then aggregates all incoming updates (McMahan et al., 2017; Abadi et al., 2016). While DP-FL’s communication rounds are independent of the number of parties, they are proportional to the number of training iterations $M$ . Moreover, DP-FL achieves a significantly weaker utility-privacy tradeoffs than central learning, already for hundreds of parties. Computation- and communication-heavy cryptographic methods can achieve the same utility-privacy tradeoffs as the centralized setting. To avoid expensive distributed noise generation protocols, each user locally adds Gaussian noise, which when summed up results in Gaussian noise. C.2 and Appx. C.3 respectively. \begin{abstract}
In this paper, we tackle the challenging task of unpaired panoramic Image-to-Image translation (Pano-I2I) for the first time. This task aims to learn a mapping between unpaired panoramic source and non-panoramic target domains to modify naive 360 panoramic images. However, it is difficult to use existing I2I methods due to two main challenges. Firstly, panoramas inherit geometric distortions, which pose challenges for methods based on a narrow field-of-view. Secondly, accessing panoramic datasets encompassing various weather conditions or times for training purposes is severely limited. To address these challenges, we propose a novel I2I model tailored for mitigating panoramic distortion that harnesses readily obtainable pinhole images as the target domain for training. We introduce a versatile encoder and distortion-free discrimination that efficiently bridges the large domain gap between panoramic and pinhole images by simultaneously encoding them in a consolidated structure. It allows our model to learn style mappings while overcoming significant geometric differences between the source and target domains. Moreover, we carefully design spherical position embedding, sphere-based rotation augmentation, and its ensemble to address the discontinuities at the panorama edges. Comprehensive experiments verify that our framework effectively translates panoramic street views from daytime to night, rainy, and twilight scenes by referring to the holistic style of pinhole data.
Our method also shows superior results in both maintaining structural coherence and rotation equivariance, clearly surpassing the existing I2I methods in qualitative and quantitative results.

\end{abstract}

\section{1 INTRODUCTION  }

Image-to-image translation (I2I) aims to modify an input image aligning with the style of the target domain, preserving the original content from the source domain. This paradigm enables numerous applications, such as colorization, style transfer, domain adaptation, data augmentation, etc (Huang et al., 2018a; Mariani et al., 2018; Murez et al., 2018; Huang & Belongie, 2017; Isola et al., 2017). However, existing I2I has been used to synthesize pinhole images with narrow field-of-view (FoV), which limits the scope of applications considering diverse image-capturing devices.  

Panoramic $360^{\circ}$ cameras have recently grown in popularity, which enables many applications, e.g., AR/VR, autonomous driving, and city map modeling (Micusik & Kosecka, 2009; Anderson et al., 2018; Caruso et al., 2015; Yogamani et al., 2019). Unlike pinhole images of narrow FoV, panoramic images (briefly, panoramas) capture the entire surroundings, providing richer information with $360^{\circ}\!\times\!180^{\circ}$ FoV. Translating panoramas into other styles can enable novel applications, such as immersive view generations or enriching user experiences with robust car-surrounding recognition (de La Garanderie et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2020; 2021b; Ma et al., 2021).  

However, naively applying conventional I2I methods for pinhole images (Park et al., 2020a; Shen et al., 2019; Choi et al., 2018; 2020; Zheng et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2021; Kim et al., 2022) to panoramas can significantly distort the geometric properties of panoramas. As existing I2I methods assume the source and target domains only differ in style conditions, they have limitations in distinguishing between style and inherent distortion where the two domains have additional geometric gaps. One may project the panoramas into pinhole images to apply the conventional methods. However, it costs considerable computation since sparse projections (Chou et al., 2018; Zhu et al., 2020) cannot cover the whole scene due to the narrow FoV of pinhole images. In addition, the discontinuity problem at edges (left-right boundaries in panorama) requires panorama-specific modeling, as in the other tasks, e.g., panorama depth estimation, panoramic segmentation, and panorama synthesis (Shen et al., 2022; Zhang et al., 2022b; Chen et al., 2022).

review.summary: The paper proposes a memory-based extension to concept bottleneck models (CBMs) to enable reusing interventions on similar data points. The proposed method, CBMM, stores the encodings of data points that the model misclassifies and the corresponding interventions. When a new data point is fed to the model, the method checks if the encoding is similar to any of the stored ones. If a similar encoding is found, the intervention is applied to the new data point. The authors evaluate the proposed method on several datasets and show that it can improve the performance of CBMs.

The idea of storing the encoding of misclassified data points and reusing interventions on similar data points is similar to the idea of storing the encoding of misclassified data points and reusing the corresponding labels in the context of active learning (e.g., [1]). The only difference is that the proposed method uses interventions instead of labels.

The proposed method is not evaluated on a diverse set of datasets. The authors only evaluate the method on a single dataset for each task. It would be better to evaluate the method on multiple datasets to show the generalization of the method.

review.summary: This paper proposes a novel zero-shot quantization framework, named ZeroP, which leverages publicly available data (proxy data) to substitute for the original data. The authors explore the impact of proxy data on the performance of current zero-shot quantization methods across 16 different computer vision datasets. They introduce a simple and effective proxy data selection method based on batch-normalization statistics (BNS) to choose the optimal proxy data. The authors apply ZeroP to three state-of-the-art pure-synthetic data methods, achieving 7% to 16% improvements in accuracy for MobileNetV1 on ImageNet-1K in a 4-bit setting. Additionally, they demonstrate the effectiveness of ZeroP on various models and datasets. The results indicate that ZeroP offers a promising solution for achieving high-performance low-bit networks without relying on original training data.

2. The authors only evaluate the proposed method on ImageNet-1K, which is a relatively small dataset. The authors should evaluate the method on larger datasets, such as ImageNet-21K, to demonstrate its effectiveness on more challenging tasks.

3. The authors should provide more details about the proxy data used in the experiments. How did the authors select the proxy data? What are the characteristics of the proxy data? How do the authors ensure that the proxy data is representative of the original data?

4. The authors should provide more analysis of the results. For example, how does the proposed method perform on different types of models? How does the proposed method perform on different tasks? What are the limitations of the proposed method?

The LLM-based knowledge can serve as robust and invariant representations, particularly in scenarios involving spatio-temporal distribution shifts. Furthermore, the spatio-temporal knowledge alignment paradigm maximizes mutual information between LLM-based knowledge representations and GNN-based structural embeddings, ensuring effective alignment and information preservation across different views. This cross-view knowledge alignment process not only facilitates effective data augmentation but also addresses inaccuracies in the raw spatio-temporal graph data by denoising noisy connections. The effectiveness of the proposed STLLM is further strengthened by theoretical analyses, demonstrating its ability to align LLM-based spatio-temporal knowledge through the maximization of mutual information. *Abstract*
A neural program induction model is considered good if it is capable of learning programs with four objectives: (1) higher data efficiency, (2) a more efficient training process, (3) better performance, and (4) generalization for large-scale tasks. However, the neural program induction/synthesis models suffer from requiring a large amount of training iterations and training examples for training. Besides, the current state-of-the-art neural program induction models are still far from perfect in terms of performance and generalization when dealing with tasks that require complex task-solving logic. To mitigate these challenges, in this work, we present a novel framework called FRGR (Failure Reflection Guided Regularizer). Our proposed framework dynamically summarizes error patterns from the model’s previous behavior and actively constrains the model from repeating mistakes of such patterns during training. In this way, the model is expected to converge faster and more data-efficiently as well as being less likely to fall into local optimum by making fewer mistakes of similar patterns. We evaluate FRGR based on multiple relational reasoning and decision-making tasks under both the data-rich and data-scarce settings. Experimental results show the effectiveness of FRGR in improving training efficiency, performance, generalization as well as data efficiency.

The authors show that in the early stage of training, the update direction of gradient descent is determined by the clean samples of training data, leaving the noisy samples to have minimal to no impact, resulting in a prioritization of clean learning. ## Reviewer
### Summary
The paper proposes a new method to find strong lottery tickets (SLT) using the edge-popup algorithm. The authors show that the standard edge-popup algorithm can lead to suboptimal solutions due to the presence of "dying edges", which are edges that are never selected during the search process.
